title: Build the database
one: The script that creates every table and fills it with sample data, and can be run again.
marks: This chapter is where the examiner looks for a database that is made by one script, with rules in the tables themselves that refuse bad data, and sample data to test with.

blocks.p: In chapter 2 you planned ten tables on paper. In this chapter you make them, by writing one script, BikeShop.sql, that the server runs from top to bottom. By the end of the chapter the script makes the database, makes the ten tables, puts in the sample data, and prints the words BikeShop is ready. Then you ask the Customer table for its rows and see twelve names come back.

blocks.p: The script has one habit that matters more than any other: it can be run again. Every time you press F5 it throws the old tables away and makes fresh ones with the same sample data. That means a mistake is never serious. If a table is wrong, you fix the script and run it again. If a test in a later chapter leaves the data in a mess, you run it again. The script is the master copy of your database, and it lives in your OneDrive folder.

words: Script
A file of SQL lines that the server runs from the top to the bottom.
Table
A grid with named columns, where each row is one thing, such as one customer.
Column
One named box in every row, with a type that says what can go in it, such as a number or a date.
Row
One line of a table: one customer, one bike, one booking.
INT
A type for whole numbers, such as 3 or 120.
VARCHAR
A type for text, with the most letters allowed in brackets, such as VARCHAR(40).
DECIMAL
A type for money and other numbers with a decimal point: DECIMAL(8,2) allows eight digits, two of them after the point.
DATE and DATETIME
DATE holds a day, such as 12 October 2026. DATETIME holds a day and a clock time together, such as 12 October 2026 at 09:30.
BIT
A type that holds a yes or a no, written as 1 or 0.
NULL
An empty box. NOT NULL after a column means the box can never be empty.
IDENTITY
The table gives each new row the next number itself, so nobody types it.
PRIMARY KEY
The column that names each row, so that no two rows can share a number.
FOREIGN KEY
A column that holds the number of a row in another table, such as the customer a booking is for.
CHECK
A rule written into the table that refuses a row that breaks it, before any program runs.
UNIQUE
A rule that no two rows can hold the same value in that column.
DEFAULT
The value a column takes when a row is added without one.
GO
A line on its own that sends everything above it to the server, so the next lines start fresh.
Sample data
Made-up rows, with real-looking names and dates, that fill the tables so that you have something to test with.

screens.title: Read why the script drops the old tables first, children before parents.

blocks.p: A script that can be run again has to deal with what is already there. The second time it runs, the ten tables exist, and CREATE TABLE would be refused with the words there is already an object named Customer. So the script starts by dropping every table it is about to make. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS means: throw the table away if it is there, and say nothing if it is not. The first run finds nothing to drop and carries on.

box.title: Children before parents
box.text: A table that holds a foreign key points at another table. Appointment points at Customer, because every booking is for one customer. Call Appointment the child and Customer the parent. The server will not drop a parent while a child still points at it, so the children go first. That is why the ten DROP TABLE lines put every child before its parent: PartSale is dropped first and Customer last, while Customer is made first and PartSale last.

blocks.p: The same order matters when the tables are made. A foreign key can only point at a table that already exists, so Customer and Staff come before Appointment, and Supplier before Part. The order in this chapter is the order that works. Keep it.

blocks.p: The top of the script does three things: it makes the database if it is not there, it moves into it, and it drops the ten old tables. Read each part, then copy the whole block into your empty BikeShop.sql and run it once. The tables come next, one at a time.

code.title: The top of BikeShop.sql: the database, and the ten DROP TABLE lines

screens.title: Read the Customer table part by part, then add it to your script.

blocks.p: The first table is Customer, and four other tables point at it. Read it slowly, because every table in this chapter is built out of the same pieces: a number column that fills itself, columns with a type and NOT NULL, a DEFAULT, a PRIMARY KEY, and a CHECK rule.

code.title: Customer: the first table
parts: The table name and its number column

CREATE TABLE and a name start the table. The bracket opens the list of columns. The first column is the number that names each row. IDENTITY(1,1) means the table gives the number out itself, starting at 1 and going up by 1, so you never type it. NOT NULL means the box can never be left empty.
Three text columns that must be filled

FirstName and LastName hold up to 40 letters each. Phone holds up to 15, because a number such as 028 3026 4411 has spaces in it and is text, not a number to add up. NOT NULL on all three: a customer with no name or no phone number is refused.
A column that may be empty
Email says NULL, not NOT NULL, so a customer without an email address can still be added. The box is left empty, and the word NULL shows in it when you look.
A date that fills itself in

DateJoined is a DATE, and it has a DEFAULT. GETDATE() gives the date and time right now, and CAST turns that into a date with no clock part. So a new customer is stamped with today's date without anyone typing it. The DEFAULT has a name, DF_Customer_DateJoined, so that an error can name it.

CustomerID is the column that names each row. PRIMARY KEY means no two customers can have the same number, and a booking can point at a customer by it. The rule is named PK_Customer: PK for primary key, then the table.

LEN counts the characters in the phone number. The CHECK refuses any row whose phone number is shorter than ten characters, so 12345 can never get in. The rule is named CK_Customer_Phone: CK for check, the table, then what it checks. The closing bracket and the semicolon end the table. GO sends everything above it to the server before the next table starts.
code.text:
CREATE TABLE Customer (
    CustomerID   INT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    FirstName    VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    LastName     VARCHAR(40)  NOT NULL,
    Phone        VARCHAR(15)   NOT NULL,
    Email        VARCHAR(100) NULL,
    DateJoined   DATE          NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_Customer_DateJoined DEFAULT (CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)),
    CONSTRAINT PK_Customer PRIMARY KEY (CustomerID),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Customer_Phone CHECK (LEN(Phone) >= 10)
);
GO

screens.title: Add the Staff table, which has a UNIQUE rule and a list of roles.

blocks.p: Staff is the people who use the program: a manager, counter staff and mechanics. Two things are new. A UNIQUE rule stops two people sharing a username, and the first CHECK with a list in it says a role must be one of three words.

code.title: Staff: the people who sign in
parts: This starts the same way as Customer: a number column that fills itself, then a first name and a last name that must be filled.
Role is one of three words, Mechanic, Counter or Manager, and it decides which screens a person can open in later chapters.

Username and Password are what a person types to sign in. The comment line is a reminder for your user guide: a real system would store a hash, which is a scrambled copy of the password that cannot be turned back into the password, and this coursework keeps it plain and says so.
BIT holds a 1 for yes or a 0 for no. The DEFAULT of 1 means a new member of staff is active unless told otherwise, and someone who leaves is set to 0 rather than deleted.
The key and the UNIQUE rule
StaffID is the primary key. UQ_Staff_Username says no two rows can have the same username, so a sign-in always finds one person.

IN followed by a list in brackets means: the value must be one of these. A role of Boss is refused by the table. The closing bracket and the semicolon end the table. GO sends everything above it to the server before the next table starts.
code.text:
CREATE TABLE Staff (
    StaffID      INT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    FirstName    VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    LastName     VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    Role         VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL,
    Username     VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL,
    -- a real system stores a hash; say so in your user guide
    Password     VARCHAR(30)  NOT NULL,
    IsActive     BIT          NOT NULL CONSTRAINT DF_Staff_IsActive DEFAULT (1),
    CONSTRAINT PK_Staff PRIMARY KEY (StaffID),
    CONSTRAINT UQ_Staff_Username UNIQUE (Username),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Staff_Role CHECK (Role IN ('Mechanic', 'Counter', 'Manager'))
);
GO

screens.title: Type the two checks of the ServiceType table.

blocks.p: ServiceType is the list of jobs the workshop does, such as a puncture repair at 15.00 for 30 minutes. It is short, so this is the table where you type the rules yourself. The copy button leaves a gap for the yellow lines, and you type them in.

code.title: ServiceType: the jobs the workshop does
parts: The table name and its number column
This starts the same way as the two tables before it, with a number that the table gives out itself.
What a job is called, how long it takes and what it costs

Name is text. DurationMinutes is a whole number of minutes. Price is DECIMAL(8,2): up to eight digits with two after the point, which is how money is stored, because a DECIMAL never rounds a penny away.
The key and the UNIQUE rule
ServiceTypeID is the primary key, and no two jobs can share a name.
The two checks: the yellow lines

BETWEEN 15 AND 480 means the length must be from a quarter of an hour to eight hours. The percent sign gives the remainder after dividing, so DurationMinutes % 15 = 0 means the length divides exactly by 15: the diary runs in quarter hours. AND joins the two tests, so both must be true. The second CHECK refuses a price below zero. The closing bracket and the semicolon end the table. GO sends everything above it to the server before the next table starts.
code.why: The two CHECK rules are the part of a table that you will write most often in your own scenario. Typing BETWEEN, the remainder sign and a comparison once, with your own hands, is how the shape sticks.
code.text:
CREATE TABLE ServiceType (
    ServiceTypeID   INT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    Name            VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    DurationMinutes INT          NOT NULL,
    Price           DECIMAL(8,2) NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT PK_ServiceType PRIMARY KEY (ServiceTypeID),
    CONSTRAINT UQ_ServiceType_Name UNIQUE (Name),
    CONSTRAINT CK_ServiceType_Duration CHECK (DurationMinutes BETWEEN 15
        AND 480 AND DurationMinutes % 15 = 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_ServiceType_Price CHECK (Price >= 0)
);
GO

    Notes           VARCHAR(200) NULL,

screens.title: Add the Bike table, which has a rule that reads two columns at once.

blocks.p: Bike is every bike the shop owns, for hire or for sale. It is the longest table, because a bike has many facts, and two of its checks read more than one column at once. Read what is new in each part, then add it.

code.title: Bike: every bike the shop owns
parts: The table name and its number column
BikeID is a number that the table gives out itself.
FrameNumber is the code stamped on the frame, such as TK-2201. Make, Model, Size and Colour are text. Size is VARCHAR(2) because the longest size, XS or XL, is two letters.
Hire or sale, and the two prices
Purpose is the word Hire or the word Sale. DailyRate and SalePrice both allow NULL, because a hire bike has no sale price and a sale bike has no daily rate.
The status, and who the bike is for
Status starts as Available. CustomerID may be empty, and holds the customer a bike is reserved for or sold to. SoldOn is the day it was sold, empty until then.
The key, the unique frame number and the foreign key
No two bikes can share a frame number, and CustomerID, when it is filled, must be a real customer.

Three lists: a size must be XS, S, M, L or XL; a purpose must be Hire or Sale; a status must be Available, Reserved, Sold or In repair. The two price checks say IS NULL OR, which means: an empty price is fine, and a filled price must not be below zero.
A hire bike needs a daily rate, a sale bike needs a price
This CHECK reads two columns at once. Either the purpose is Hire and the daily rate is filled, or the purpose is Sale and the sale price is filled. A sale bike with no price is refused.
A sold bike needs a date and a customer

Either the status is Sold and both the day and the customer are filled, or the status is anything else and the day is empty. The two-character sign <> means is not equal to. The closing bracket and the semicolon end the table. GO sends everything above it to the server before the next table starts.

CREATE TABLE Bike (
    BikeID      INT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    FrameNumber VARCHAR(20)  NOT NULL,
    Make        VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
    Model       VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    Size        VARCHAR(2)   NOT NULL,
    Colour      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    Purpose     VARCHAR(4)   NOT NULL,
    DailyRate   DECIMAL(6,2) NULL,
    SalePrice   DECIMAL(8,2) NULL,
    Status      VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_Bike_Status DEFAULT ('Available'),
    CustomerID  INT          NULL,      -- reserved for / sold to
    SoldOn      DATE         NULL,
    CONSTRAINT PK_Bike PRIMARY KEY (BikeID),
    CONSTRAINT UQ_Bike_FrameNumber UNIQUE (FrameNumber),
    CONSTRAINT FK_Bike_Customer FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID)
        REFERENCES Customer (CustomerID),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Bike_Size    CHECK (Size IN ('XS', 'S', 'M', 'L', 'XL')),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Bike_Purpose CHECK (Purpose IN ('Hire', 'Sale')),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Bike_Status  CHECK (Status IN ('Available', 'Reserved',
        'Sold', 'In repair')),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Bike_DailyRate CHECK (DailyRate IS NULL OR DailyRate >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Bike_SalePrice CHECK (SalePrice IS NULL OR SalePrice >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Bike_PriceForPurpose CHECK (
        (Purpose = 'Hire' AND DailyRate IS NOT NULL)
            OR (Purpose = 'Sale' AND SalePrice IS NOT NULL)),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Bike_SoldNeedsDetails CHECK (
        (Status = 'Sold' AND SoldOn IS NOT NULL AND CustomerID IS NOT NULL)
            OR (Status <> 'Sold' AND SoldOn IS NULL))
);
GO

screens.title: Add the Hire table, and read the deposit check.

blocks.p: Hire is one row per bike hire: which bike, which customer, the day it goes out and the day it comes back. Most of it you have seen before. Read the deposit check with care, because it is the shape of every money rule in your own scenario.

code.title: Hire: one row per bike hire
parts: The number column and two pointers
HireID is given out by the table. BikeID and CustomerID are the numbers of a real bike and a real customer.
A hire is by the day, not the hour, so both are DATE with no clock part. The comment says what EndDate means: the day the bike comes back.
TotalCost is what the hire costs. DepositPaid is what was paid up front, and it starts at 0 unless a value is given.
The status, who booked it and when
Status is Booked until told otherwise. BookedByStaffID is the staff member who took the booking, and BookedOn is the date and time it was made, stamped by GETDATE().
The key and three foreign keys
HireID names the row. The three FOREIGN KEY rules say the bike, the customer and the staff member must each be a real row in their own table.
The bike must come back after it goes out, and the total cost cannot be below zero.

CONSTRAINT names the rule: CK for check, Hire for the table, Deposit for what it checks. CHECK opens the test. Inside the brackets, DepositPaid >= 0 is true for a deposit of 0 or more and false for a deposit of minus 5. When the test is false, the row is refused and the red text names CK_Hire_Deposit. A program never gets the chance to store a negative deposit.
Status must be Booked, Out, Returned or Cancelled, and nothing else. The closing bracket and the semicolon end the table. GO sends everything above it to the server before the next table starts.

    HireID          INT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    BikeID          INT          NOT NULL,
    CustomerID      INT          NOT NULL,
    StartDate       DATE         NOT NULL,
    EndDate         DATE         NOT NULL,   -- the day the bike comes back
    TotalCost       DECIMAL(8,2) NOT NULL,
    DepositPaid     DECIMAL(8,2) NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_Hire_DepositPaid DEFAULT (0),
    Status          VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_Hire_Status DEFAULT ('Booked'),
    BookedByStaffID INT          NOT NULL,
    BookedOn        DATETIME     NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_Hire_BookedOn DEFAULT (GETDATE()),
    CONSTRAINT PK_Hire PRIMARY KEY (HireID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_Hire_Bike     FOREIGN KEY (BikeID)
        REFERENCES Bike (BikeID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_Hire_Customer FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID)
        REFERENCES Customer (CustomerID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_Hire_BookedBy FOREIGN KEY (BookedByStaffID)
        REFERENCES Staff (StaffID),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Hire_Dates   CHECK (EndDate > StartDate),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Hire_Total   CHECK (TotalCost >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Hire_Deposit CHECK (DepositPaid >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Hire_Status  CHECK (Status IN ('Booked', 'Out', 'Returned',
        'Cancelled'))
);
GO

screens.title: Write the Part table yourself, with the rule that stock can never go below zero.

blocks.p: Part is every part on the shelf: what it is called, who supplies it, what the shop pays, what the customer pays, and how many are in stock. It has one foreign key, to Supplier, and five CHECK rules. One of those rules is the most important line in this whole script for chapter 8, where parts are sold: stock can never go below zero. Write the table from the plan, run it, then compare.

parts: The table name and its number column
PartID is a number that the table gives out itself.
The code, the name and the supplier
PartCode is the short code on the shelf label, such as TUBE-700. Name is what a person reads. SupplierID points at Supplier.
UnitCost is what the shop pays the supplier, and SellPrice is what the customer pays. Both are DECIMAL(7,2), so the pennies are exact. The comments say which is which.
How many, and when to order more
QtyInStock starts at 0 by DEFAULT. ReorderLevel is the count at which more should be ordered, and ReorderQty is how many to order then. Chapter 8 uses both.

PartID names the row, no two parts share a code, and the supplier must be a real row in Supplier.
These are two checks of the same shape as the deposit check in Hire.
Stock can never go below zero

The reorder level may be 0, meaning never reorder. The reorder quantity must be more than 0, because ordering nothing makes no sense. The closing bracket and the semicolon end the table. GO sends everything above it to the server before the next table starts.

CREATE TABLE Part (
    PartID       INT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    PartCode     VARCHAR(12)  NOT NULL,
    Name         VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL,
    SupplierID   INT          NOT NULL,
    UnitCost     DECIMAL(7,2) NOT NULL,   -- what we pay
    SellPrice    DECIMAL(7,2) NOT NULL,   -- what the customer pays
    QtyInStock   INT          NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_Part_QtyInStock DEFAULT (0),
    ReorderLevel INT          NOT NULL,
    ReorderQty   INT          NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT PK_Part PRIMARY KEY (PartID),
    CONSTRAINT UQ_Part_PartCode UNIQUE (PartCode),
    CONSTRAINT FK_Part_Supplier FOREIGN KEY (SupplierID)
        REFERENCES Supplier (SupplierID),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Part_UnitCost     CHECK (UnitCost >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Part_SellPrice    CHECK (SellPrice >= 0),
    -- stock can never go below zero
    CONSTRAINT CK_Part_QtyInStock   CHECK (QtyInStock >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Part_ReorderLevel CHECK (ReorderLevel >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_Part_ReorderQty   CHECK (ReorderQty > 0)
);
GO

screens.title: Add the PartOrder table, which records orders to suppliers.

blocks.p: PartOrder is one row per order the shop places with a supplier for more of a part. Nothing in it is new except that three of its columns stay empty until the order arrives. Read what each part does, then add it.

code.title: PartOrder: one row per order to a supplier
parts: The number, the part and how many
PartOrderID is given out by the table. PartID points at the part. QtyOrdered is how many were asked for.
OrderedOn is a DATE that its DEFAULT stamps with today, using the same CAST of GETDATE() as DateJoined in Customer.
Three columns that wait for the delivery
ExpectedOn, ReceivedOn and QtyReceived all allow NULL, because an order that has not arrived yet has no delivery day and no count received.
The status, and who placed it
Status starts as Ordered until something changes it, and PlacedByStaffID is the number of the member of staff who placed the order.
The key and two foreign keys
The part must be a real row in Part, and the staff member a real row in Staff.
QtyOrdered must be more than 0. QtyReceived may be empty, and when it is filled it must be 0 or more.
Status must be Ordered, Received or Cancelled. The closing bracket and the semicolon end the table. GO sends everything above it to the server before the next table starts.

CREATE TABLE PartOrder (
    PartOrderID     INT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    PartID          INT         NOT NULL,
    QtyOrdered      INT         NOT NULL,
    OrderedOn       DATE        NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_PartOrder_OrderedOn DEFAULT (CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE)),
    ExpectedOn      DATE        NULL,
    ReceivedOn      DATE        NULL,
    QtyReceived     INT         NULL,
    Status          VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_PartOrder_Status DEFAULT ('Ordered'),
    PlacedByStaffID INT         NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT PK_PartOrder PRIMARY KEY (PartOrderID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_PartOrder_Part     FOREIGN KEY (PartID)
        REFERENCES Part (PartID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_PartOrder_PlacedBy FOREIGN KEY (PlacedByStaffID)
        REFERENCES Staff (StaffID),
    CONSTRAINT CK_PartOrder_Qty         CHECK (QtyOrdered > 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_PartOrder_QtyReceived CHECK (QtyReceived IS NULL
        OR QtyReceived >= 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_PartOrder_Status      CHECK (Status IN ('Ordered', 'Received',
        'Cancelled'))
);
GO

screens.title: Add the PartSale table, the last of the ten.

blocks.p: PartSale is one row per sale of a part over the counter. Two things are new: a customer column that may be empty, because many people who buy an inner tube are not on the books, and a price column that keeps the price on the day, so that a later price change does not rewrite history.

code.title: PartSale: one row per sale over the counter
parts: PartSaleID is given out by the table. PartID points at the part that was sold.
The customer, who may be a walk-in, and how many
CustomerID allows NULL. The comment says why: an empty box means a walk-in customer, someone not on the books. Quantity is how many were sold.
The price on the day, and when
UnitPrice is copied from the part's SellPrice at the moment of the sale, so a price rise next month does not change what was paid today. SoldOn is stamped with the date and time by GETDATE().
Who sold it, and the status
SoldByStaffID is the number of the member of staff at the counter, and Status starts as Sold.
The key and three foreign keys
The part, the customer when there is one, and the staff member must each be a real row in their own table.

A sale of 0 or fewer parts is refused, and the status must be Sold or Refunded. The closing bracket and the semicolon end the table. GO sends everything above it to the server before the next table starts.
code.text:
CREATE TABLE PartSale (
    PartSaleID    INT IDENTITY(1,1) NOT NULL,
    PartID        INT          NOT NULL,
    CustomerID    INT          NULL,      -- NULL = walk-in customer
    Quantity      INT          NOT NULL,
    -- the price on the day: history keeps it
    UnitPrice     DECIMAL(7,2) NOT NULL,
    SoldOn        DATETIME     NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_PartSale_SoldOn DEFAULT (GETDATE()),
    SoldByStaffID INT          NOT NULL,
    Status        VARCHAR(10)  NOT NULL
        CONSTRAINT DF_PartSale_Status DEFAULT ('Sold'),
    CONSTRAINT PK_PartSale PRIMARY KEY (PartSaleID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_PartSale_Part     FOREIGN KEY (PartID)
        REFERENCES Part (PartID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_PartSale_Customer FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID)
        REFERENCES Customer (CustomerID),
    CONSTRAINT FK_PartSale_SoldBy   FOREIGN KEY (SoldByStaffID)
        REFERENCES Staff (StaffID),
    CONSTRAINT CK_PartSale_Quantity CHECK (Quantity > 0),
    CONSTRAINT CK_PartSale_Status   CHECK (Status IN ('Sold', 'Refunded'))
);
GO

screens.title: Read the Customer INSERT, and what @Today does.

blocks.p: Every table is filled the same way: INSERT INTO, the table name, the list of columns in brackets, VALUES, then one row per bracket. Read the Customer one. The one thing that is not a plain value is @Today. A name beginning with @ is a variable: a named box that holds one value while the script runs. The lines above the INSERT in your script declare @Today and set it to today's date with CAST(GETDATE() AS DATE). Every DateJoined is counted back from that box, so the sample customers always joined between 400 and 5 days ago, whatever day you run the script. Two more boxes, @Day0 and @Next, do the same for the bookings, so that the diary always has bookings tomorrow.

code.title: INSERT INTO Customer: the twelve sample customers
parts: The five columns named in the brackets are the ones given a value, in that order. CustomerID is not in the list, because the table gives it out itself. VALUES says the rows follow.

One row is one bracket with five values in the column order: Aoife, McCann, a phone number in quotes because it is text, an email address, and a date. DATEADD(DAY, -400, @Today) means: take the date in the @Today box and go back 400 days. The comment line with the number 1 is a note for a person, so that you can count the rows.

blocks.p: Every row below is a test the examiner would run, and the last two are the ones that matter most. A table with a CHECK rule refuses a bad row by itself, with red text that names the rule, before any program exists. You type each refused INSERT into your New Query window, over the SELECT, and the red text is the evidence. Nothing is added, and SELECT * FROM Customer; afterwards still shows twelve rows. Take a screenshot of each refusal while its red text is on the screen, and another of the twelve rows. A screenshot is a picture of what is on the screen. To take one, click the Start button, type Snipping Tool, and press Enter to open it. Press New, drag a box round the red text or the rows, press Ctrl and S together, type a name such as refusal-1 or customers, and save it in your OneDrive coursework folder, the same folder as BikeShop.sql.

screens.title: Finish the chapter.

blocks.p: Five ticks are your evidence that one script makes the whole database, that it can be run again, and that the rules in the tables refuse bad rows before any program is written. Keep your screenshots of the two red refusals and of the twelve customers for your testing evidence in chapter 10. Close the New Query window by clicking the small cross on its tab. When it asks whether to save the changes, click No: the script is the only file that matters, and it is saved in your OneDrive folder.

box.title: Make it yours
box.text: Your scenario has its own ten tables from chapter 2. Build them in this order: every table that points at nothing first, then the tables that point at those, then the rest, and drop them in the opposite order at the top. Give every rule a name in the same shape, PK, FK, UQ, CK or DF, then the table, then what it is about, so that every red refusal tells you which rule spoke. Write at least one CHECK with a list of allowed words, one that compares two columns, and one that says a count can never go below zero. Then make your own sample data, with at least ten rows in your busiest table, and dates counted back from @Today.
